```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(knbsdata)
```

County-level work in Kenya lives or dies on join keys. This vignette covers
the reference codes `knbs_geographies()` provides, the two mistakes that
silently corrupt county joins, and what this package deliberately does not
offer.

Chunks that contact the service are shown but not run.

## The reference

```{r, eval = FALSE}
geo <- knbs_geographies()
counties <- knbs_geographies(level = "county")
mombasa_subs <- knbs_geographies(parent = "01")
```

One row per territorial unit of the 2019 Population and Housing Census frame:
Kenya (`"00"`), 47 counties (`"01"`–`"47"`), and their sub-counties (four
digits, the first two being the county). Names, levels and parent codes come
with it, read live from the census service (CC BY 4.0) rather than shipped as
a snapshot that could drift from the source.

## The two classic corruptions

**Leading zeros.** County codes are character, and `"01"` is not `1`. The
moment a code passes through `as.numeric()` — or through a CSV round-trip
that guesses types — Mombasa (`"01"`) collides with nothing and matches
nothing. Everything in this package keeps codes as character; keep them that
way in your own pipelines, and if you read codes from a file, read that
column as character explicitly.

**Vintage mixing.** These are the *2019 census frame* units. Administrative
units change: joining 2019 codes against a table coded to another frame will
drop or misassign rows without erroring. The `vintage` column exists so that
the frame travels with the data; check it before joining anything that did
not come from this package.

## A worked join

County population against the reference, giving each county its share:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pop <- knbs_get_indicator("POPCEN0001", geo_level = "county")
totals <- pop[pop$sex == "total" & pop$marital_status == "Total",
              c("geo_code", "geo_name", "value")]

geo <- knbs_geographies(level = "county")
joined <- merge(totals, geo[, c("geo_code", "parent_code")], by = "geo_code")

joined$share <- joined$value / sum(joined$value)
head(joined[order(-joined$share), ])
```

The join is exact by construction: observations and reference use the same
codes from the same source.

## Gross County Product

KNBS publishes the size of each county's economy, the Gross County Product,
in a report each year, as tables printed in a PDF. `knbs_gcp()` reads them
from the KNBS publications library by curated recipe and returns them
already coded to the census counties:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gcp <- knbs_gcp()                          # current prices, latest edition
real <- knbs_gcp(prices = "constant")      # constant 2016 prices
shares <- knbs_gcp("share")                # percent of gross value added

latest <- gcp[gcp$period == 2024 & gcp$geo_code != "00", ]
head(latest[order(-latest$value), c("county", "value", "status")])
```

Every read checks the table: all 47 counties and the total present once,
the counties adding up to the total within rounding, and figures checked by
hand at curation unchanged. A report that has changed is refused rather
than misread.

Three things to know, all in `knbs_metadata()`:

- **Each edition revises the years before it.** `edition = "latest"` (the
  default) gives the newest; `edition = "all"` gives every edition, one
  block each, so revisions can be compared. The editions curated are 2019,
  2021, 2023, 2024 and 2025, together covering 2013–2024.
- **Constant prices changed base year.** The 2019 edition values them at
  2009 prices; from 2021 they are 2016 prices, after the national accounts
  were rebased. The `base_year` column says which. Never splice the two
  into one series.
- **The newest year is provisional**: `status` is `"provisional"` where the
  report marks a year with an asterisk.

Because the counties carry census codes, GCP joins every other county table
in the package directly — per-capita GCP against the reports' own county
population tables, for instance:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pop <- knbs_county_population()
pop <- pop[pop$measure == "population_projected", c("geo_code", "period", "value")]
names(pop)[3] <- "population"
per_head <- merge(gcp[, c("geo_code", "county", "period", "value")], pop,
                  by = c("geo_code", "period"))
per_head$gcp_per_head <- per_head$value * 1e6 / per_head$population
```

`knbs_report_tables()` lists every curated table with its edition, prices
and base year; `knbs_report_table()` returns any one of them exactly as
printed, including the reports' averages.

## County budgets and spending

`knbs_county_budget()` gives each county's approved budget and actual
spending, recurrent and development, its absorption rates, spending by
economic classification, own-source revenue against target, pending bills
and exchequer issues, from the Office of the Controller of Budget's annual
budget implementation review reports, FY 2013/14 to 2023/24:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
budget <- knbs_county_budget()
dev <- knbs_county_budget(measure = c("budget_development", "expenditure_development"))
knbs_county_budget(county = "Turkana", measure = "absorption_development")
knbs_county_budget(measure = c("osr_target", "osr_actual"))
knbs_county_budget(measure = "pending_total")
```

Own-source revenue deserves care. `osr_actual` is what a county collected
and `osr_target` what it budgeted to collect, and they are not the same
thing: the figures on the KNBS Data Portal (`DF_PF_CG_REV`) are actual
collections in only some years. In FY 2023/24 the Controller of Budget's
totals include facility improvement funds and appropriations-in-aid that
earlier years leave out, so use `osr_actual_ordinary` to compare across
years.

The `status` column says how far to trust a figure as it stands: `NA` as
printed, `"derived"` computed from other figures, `"misprint"` or
`"inconsistent"` kept as the report prints it though it fails its own
arithmetic, and `"not_reported"` for a county that did not submit figures.

The Controller of Budget's website answers programs with a bot check, so
these figures ship with the package; they were read from the reports by the
same curated recipes and checks as every report table, including the
identity each row must satisfy (total = recurrent + development). Money is
in KSh million throughout. Fiscal years are labelled as the reports label
them (`"2023/24"`); GCP and population are calendar years, so decide how to
align the two before joining them. FY 2013/14 reports spending by arm of
government (County Assembly, County Executive); its overall totals are
derived from that split and marked `status = "derived"`.

A copy of any of the reports can be re-read, and checked, with
`knbs_report_table("cob-2023-24-budget", file = "path/to/report.pdf")`.

## Health by county: the KDHS

The Kenya Demographic and Health Survey has reported its indicators for all
47 counties since 2014. The DHS Program publishes them (`source_id`
`"dhs_program"`), and the package gives the county rows census codes, so
they join census tables directly:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
stunting <- knbs_get_indicator("CN_NUTS_C_HA2", geo_level = "county")
pop <- knbs_get_indicator("POPCEN0002", geo_level = "county")
pop <- pop[pop$age_type == "total" & pop$sex == "total", c("geo_code", "value")]

joined <- merge(stunting[stunting$period == 2022, ], pop, by = "geo_code",
                suffixes = c("", "_population"))
head(joined[order(-joined$value), c("geo_name", "value", "value_population")], 3)
#>      geo_name value value_population
#> 3      Kilifi  37.0          1440770
#> 24 West Pokot  33.5           618761
#> 25    Samburu  31.4           307946
```

Three things to know. A county appears only where the survey's sample
supports a county estimate: most indicators cover all 47, some only the
counties where the question applies (malaria treatment in the lake-endemic
counties, for instance). The surveys before 2014 report the eight former
provinces instead, at `geo_level` `"region"` with no code, since no census
code exists for a province. And Nairobi is both a province and a county:
where the survey lists it once, at its county level, it is a county row.

## Matching county names across sources

County names are not spelled alike even within KNBS: the census writes
"Murang'a", "Tharaka-Nithi" and "Nairobi City", the Data Portal "MURANGA",
"THARAKA NITHI" and "NAIROBI", under codes of its own (`KE_200_MU`).
Treasury, Controller of Budget and survey data add their own variants.
`knbs_county_code()` turns any of them into the census codes:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
knbs_county_code(c("Murang'a", "MURANGA", "Nairobi City County",
                   "taita/taveta", "Homabay", "47"))
#> [1] "21" "21" "47" "06" "43" "47"
```

Matching sets aside case, punctuation, spacing, apostrophes and the words
"County", "City" and "Government"; numbers 1 to 47 are county numbers;
"Kenya" is `"00"`. Nothing else is matched — there is no list of
alternative names to guess from — so a misspelling becomes `NA` with a
warning that names it and suggests the nearest official name:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
knbs_county_code("Kakamenga")
#> Warning: 1 value matched no county and became `NA`:
#> • "Kakamenga" (did you mean "Kakamega"?)

knbs_match_counties(c("Kakamenga", "Uasin-Gishu", "07"))   # how each matched
```

That makes cross-source joins one line. The rural share of each county's
population, from the Data Portal's rural table and the census:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(dplyr)

rural <- knbs_get_indicator("DF_POP_CENSUS_RUR", source = "knbs_opendata") |>
  filter(indic_phc_code == "POP_TOT", sex == "total", geo_code != "KE") |>
  mutate(county_code = knbs_county_code(geo_name))     # "MURANGA" -> "21"

total <- knbs_get_indicator("POPCEN0002", geo_level = "county") |>
  filter(sex == "total", age_type == "total")

rural |>
  inner_join(total, by = c(county_code = "geo_code"),
             suffix = c("_rural", "_total")) |>
  mutate(rural_share = value_rural / value_total) |>
  arrange(desc(rural_share))
#> Bomet 0.97, Kitui 0.96, Elgeyo/Marakwet 0.96, ... Kiambu 0.30;
#> Nairobi City and Mombasa NA: the portal reports no rural population there.
```

All 48 names the portal uses (47 counties and KENYA) match, to 48 distinct
codes.

## What is deliberately absent

- **Other vintages and crosswalks.** Only the 2019 frame has a verified
  source. `knbs_geographies(vintage = 2009)` fails with a clear error rather
  than serving an unverified concordance — a wrong crosswalk is worse than
  none.
- **Boundaries.** `knbs_boundaries()` does not exist. No officially licensed,
  redistributable boundary file has been verified, and the plan implements
  boundaries only after that review.
- **Classifications.** Industry, occupation and product classifications have
  no audited source yet.

If you know an official source for any of these, a
[data source change issue](https://github.com/Mustapha-Wasseja/knbsdata/issues/new/choose)
is the right place to point at it.
